claims.text: Equiatomic NbMoTaW has a single-phase BCC structure.
Equiatomic NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical strength at approximately 1600 °C.
Equiatomic NbMoTaW has very poor room-temperature ductility.
Adding approximately 0.5 at% Hf to NbMoTaW will produce Hf-rich nanoscale precipitates or clusters.
The Hf-rich precipitates will be finely dispersed and coherent within a continuous BCC matrix.
Trace Hf will segregate to particular lattice sites or grain boundaries in NbMoTaW.
Hf-rich precipitates will facilitate dislocation motion and activate additional slip at room temperature.
The Hf-induced microstructure will inhibit brittle fracture and significantly increase room-temperature strain to failure.
At high temperature, the Hf-rich precipitates will obstruct dislocation glide and help maintain yield strength.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance close to 1600 °C relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
Hf-rich precipitates will trap or promote recombination of irradiation-induced point defects.
Adding approximately 0.5 at% Hf will preserve the irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW.
The beneficial regime is limited to trace Hf concentrations around or below 0.5 at%.
Higher Hf concentrations may cause excessive precipitation or phase separation.
Excessive Hf-induced precipitation or phase separation may reduce high-temperature strength or cause embrittlement.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires Hf-rich precipitates within the BCC matrix, while the experiment says both alloys will be processed to achieve a single-phase BCC microstructure. Distinct precipitates would ordinarily make the modified material multiphase unless they are merely compositionally enriched clusters that retain the same BCC phase.
